total.tierNotes: Simple tier 7.0. S1 (9.5) is the tier ideal: single-turn inline Python palindrome, punctuation/case handled via isalnum+lower (historical failure fixed), honest edge docs, no files, no scope creep. S2 and S3 (6.5 each) share one defining regression: both wrote unrequested test files against explicit no-tests prompts — S3's thinking even acknowledged no tests were requested, then wrote 12 anyway. S2's queue is semantically correct (O(1) head/tail, RangeError throw paths, clean export) but adds an unrequested size getter and burned 14 turns on ESM import-extension churn caused solely by the unrequested test file. S3's debounce has correct trailing-edge semantics (timer reset, last-call args/this, async wait=0) but adds unrequested .cancel() and wait-validation API, and its sleep-based tests lack the deterministic-clock seam. No observable-semantics bugs anywhere in the tier — all deductions are restraint-pattern (unrequested tests x2, unrequested API x2, turn churn), which is why the weighted score sits at 7.0 rather than the 6.5 median.

Unrequested test file despite prompt asking for no tests — thinking assumed 'with tests' from turn one
14 turns burned on ESM import-extension churn, entirely self-inflicted by the unrequested test file

Unrequested RangeError validation of wait (extra behavior surface, documented as API)

Tests rely on real 30-60ms sleeps, not deterministic timing (the seam anchor C2 was rewarded for)

C1_lruCache.qualityNotes: C1 median 8.0 (runs 8.5/8.0/7.5). All three runs: sentinel doubly-linked list, genuine O(1), correct eviction semantics on all adversarial probes (update-of-existing promotes to MRU, get promotes, capacity-1, clear+reuse) — no wrapper/juggling bugs found. Common mild scope creep: unrequested size getter (all), public readonly capacity (r1/r2); all extra surface is tested, so lighter ding than the untested has() on the 7.5 anchor. r1 (8.5): 53 assertions, NaN capacity + message-content throw tests, size-tracking suite; ding: JSON.stringify fallback equality. r2 (8.0): exact-error-type throw tests; dings: no NaN test, detach leaves stale pointers. r3 (7.5): leanest API but assertThrows ignores its msgFragment param and passes on any exception (throw tests validate nothing about error type), plus a leftover confused comment in a test. JSDoc honest in all three.

C2_rateLimiter.qualityNotes: C2 median 8.0 (runs: 8.0 / 8.5 / 6.0). r2 best: deterministic exact-assertion time tests with zero sleeps (via Date.now monkeypatch+try/finally, not a proper injectable now() seam) plus Number.isFinite guards and throw-path tests — fixes both 8.5-anchor residuals but swaps in a global-stub hack and one latent strict-equality flake under the real clock. r1 solid (isFinite guards, typed throw tests, clean API) but keeps a real 120ms sleep with tolerance assertions — no clock seam. r3 regresses to the v1-C2 hole: bare <=0 validation lets NaN/Infinity poison the bucket permanently, AND its sync test runner never awaits its two async timing tests, so their pass status is fake (counted passed before assertions run); only its typed throw-path tests keep it above v1's 5.5. Universal residual across all three runs: consume(tokens>capacity) is silently false forever and undocumented; none test NaN/Infinity inputs. No scope creep anywhere (r2's public readonly rate/capacity is the only extra surface). Pattern: the injectable-clock-seam lesson from the tuned baseline did not consistently transfer — 1 of 3 runs achieved determinism, 0 of 3 via a real seam.

C3_eventEmitter.qualityNotes: C3 median 8.5 (r1 8.5, r2 6.5, r3 8.5). r1/r3 use the robust Entry{original,wrapper} per-event design: correct on every probe AND every corner (duplicate once, cross-event once), zero scope creep — held under 9.0 only because each tests just one direction of mid-dispatch mutation (r1 add-during, r3 removal-during) and neither tests re-entrancy, vs the v1 anchor that tested everything; all three runs retain the historical Record<string,unknown> interface-rejection ding (r1 even comments on it without fixing). r2 is the cautionary tale: a global Map<original,wrapper> for once bookkeeping means duplicate once(fn) or once(fn) on two events leaves an unremovable wrapper that refires forever and defeats off() — contradicting its own JSDoc — while its otherwise best-in-class 21-assert suite (only run testing re-entrant emit) never touches those paths. Pattern: forge reliably nails the probed danger zones and restraint (no extra API in any run), but wrapper-bookkeeping data-structure choice is the remaining variance axis, and self-test coverage of snapshot/aliasing corners is inconsistent across runs.

dings: No injectable clock seam — tests use real Thread.sleep(100/200) with wide tolerance bands (5.0..15.0 for expected ~10), the precise defect that separated the 8.5 tuned-C2 anchor (deterministic exact assertions) from the 5.5 v1-C2 anchor; timing-jitter flakiness risk is real

consume(tokens > burstCapacity) is silently false forever — never documented as unsatisfiable and never tested (same class of ding as v1 C2, though the generic 'false when insufficient' doc makes it milder here)
Unrequested thread-safety (@Synchronized) is mild scope creep — the prompt (mirroring C2) never asked for it; honest but unasked-for surface per rubric
Infinity slips through validation: rate=POSITIVE_INFINITY and burstCapacity=POSITIVE_INFINITY both pass require(); no Infinity tests
assertThrows catches bare Exception rather than IllegalArgumentException, so throw-path tests would pass on any exception type

Retain-cycle memory leak — the exact Swift danger zone the rubric names: LRUNode holds STRONG prev and strong next, so every adjacent node pair is a strong reference cycle; remove() nils links on eviction, but clear() only resets the sentinels (head.next=tail, tail.prev=head) leaving the interior chain n1<->n2<->... mutually retained — every clear() with >=2 entries leaks all nodes, and cache deinit leaks the whole chain the same way; a long-lived cache calling clear() periodically leaks unboundedly (LRUCache.swift:13-14, 166-171)

The leak directly contradicts clear()'s own doc comment ('iterates the dictionary to release references' — the node chain is never released), echoing the untuned-C3 'contradicts its own JSDoc' pattern at lower severity
None of the 41 tests probe deallocation (a weak-reference-goes-nil-after-clear test is feasible in the file-runner setup), so the broken case is exactly the one the suite never touches
Reference-type choice (final class) and the sentinel-forced Key?/Value? optionality are undocumented rationale — rubric asks for the value-vs-reference decision to be stated
Minor unrequested API surface: public count and public capacity beyond the requested get/put/clear (mild; both tested)

platformTasks.tierNotes: Platform tier (C4 Kotlin + C5 Swift): task 7.0 (mean of c4=7.5, c5=6.5). C4 (7.5): correct token-bucket semantics on a monotonic System.nanoTime base, idiomatic require() that incidentally rejects NaN, throw-path tests present, capacity-cap tested, tight API restraint; held back by no injectable clock seam (real Thread.sleep tests with ±5-token tolerance — the 8.5-vs-5.5 anchor differentiator), undocumented+untested consume(>capacity) forever-false, Infinity passing validation, and mild unrequested @Synchronized scope creep (claim is honest, synchronization is real). C5 (6.5): functionally flawless LRU (promote-on-get/update, sentinel DLL, capacity-1, clear-reuse) with excellent 41-assertion danger-zone suite and idiomatic Swift API, but commits the rubric's named Swift sin: strong prev AND next pointers make every adjacent node pair a retain cycle — clear() only relinks the sentinels, so clear() with >=2 entries and cache deinit both leak the entire node chain, contradicting clear()'s own 'release references' doc; the suite never probes deallocation. Pattern vs anchors: forge continues to nail observable semantics and throw-path/danger-zone functional coverage but misses the per-platform resource/determinism seam (no clock injection in Kotlin, no weak back-pointer in Swift) — the invisible-to-green-tests defect class.

overallQuality.basis: Equal-weight mean of 4 graded units matching the historical tuned-baseline basis: C1 task score 8.0 (median of 8.5/8.0/7.5), C2 task score 8.0 (median of 8.0/8.5/6.0; skeptic upheld c2_r3 at 6.0 with no adjustment), C3 task score 8.5 (median of 8.5/6.5/8.5), simple-tier score 7.0 (restraint-weighted; s1 skeptic upheld at 9.5). Platform tier (C4 7.5, C5 6.5, tier 7.0) reported separately, excluded from headline per instructions. (8.0+8.0+8.5+7.0)/4 = 7.875.
strengths: Observable-semantics correctness is now the norm on complex tasks: all 3 C1 runs use a genuine O(1) sentinel DLL with correct promotion/eviction on every adversarial probe, and 2 of 3 C3 runs use the structurally correct Entry{original,wrapper} per-event design that handles duplicate-once and cross-event-once aliasing (the exact bug class that sank untuned C3 at 5.0)
Throw-path testing — a residual gap even on the 8.5 tuned-C2 anchor — is now present in every C1/C2 run and in the Kotlin C4 run, including error-type and message-content assertions in the best runs
NaN/Infinity input validation (Number.isFinite) landed in 2 of 3 C2 runs and incidentally in Kotlin via require(rate > 0.0), closing the historical v1-C2 poisoning hole in most runs
API restraint on complex tasks is strong: zero unrequested methods in any C3 run, near-zero in C2; extra surface elsewhere is minor (size/capacity getters) and always tested

Danger-zone test coverage is dense and real where it exists: 53 assertions on C1 r1, a 41-assertion Swift suite, and C3 r3's mid-dispatch-removal ordering test — the strongest single adversarial test across all runs
S1 (9.5) is the restraint ideal: single-turn inline answer fixing the exact historical punctuation/case failure, honest edge docs, no files, no scope creep
weaknesses: The injectable clock seam — the defining lesson of the 8.5 tuned-C2 anchor — did not transfer: 0 of 4 timing-dependent artifacts (C2 x3, C4) used a real now() seam; only c2_r2 achieved determinism, via a global Date.now monkeypatch with a latent strict-equality flake, while c2_r3 and C4 rely on real sleeps with tolerance bands

High run-to-run variance with a low-tail failure mode each complex task: c2_r3 (6.0) regresses to the full v1 NaN/Infinity poisoning hole plus a sync runner that fake-passes its two async timing tests; c3_r2 (6.5) has a global once-wrapper map making listeners refire forever, contradicting its own JSDoc

Simple-tier restraint regression: S2 and S3 both wrote unrequested test files against explicit no-tests prompts (S3's thinking acknowledged the boundary then crossed it), plus unrequested size/.cancel()/validation API and 14 turns of self-inflicted ESM churn on S2

Platform-specific resource/determinism seams are the invisible-to-green-tests blind spot: Swift C5 commits the rubric's named sin (strong prev+next pointers → retain cycles; clear() and deinit leak the entire node chain, contradicting clear()'s own doc) and none of its 41 tests probe deallocation
The consume(tokens>capacity) silently-false-forever, undocumented residual persists in all 3 C2 runs and C4 — a v1-era ding never addressed anywhere

Historical dings acknowledged but not fixed: all 3 C3 runs keep the Record<string,unknown> constraint rejecting interface event maps (r1 even comments on it); several test helpers (c1_r3 assertThrows, c2_r2, C4) accept any thrown type, weakening throw-path validation they nominally provide
overallQuality.comparisonToTuned783: 7.88 vs 7.83 — statistical parity, a +0.05 nudge on the identical 4-unit basis (C1, C2, C3, simple tier). Composition shifted rather than improved: complex-task ceilings rose (C1 8.0 vs anchor 7.5 — import side effects and untested surface eliminated; C3 8.5 with two structurally correct runs; C2 median holds 8.0 with NaN guards and throw-path tests that the 8.5 anchor lacked), but two anchor lessons failed to transfer — the injectable clock seam (0/4 real seams vs the anchor's clean implementation) and simple-tier restraint (unrequested test files on 2 of 3 explicit no-tests prompts, dragging the tier to 7.0). Run variance is the real story the headline hides: best runs beat the tuned baseline, worst runs (c2_r3 6.0, c3_r2 6.5) fall to near-v1 territory. Platform tier (7.0, not in either headline) shows the same pattern extends cross-language: correct semantics, missing per-platform seam (no clock injection in Kotlin, retain cycles in Swift). Verdict: at parity overall, better at observable semantics and throw-path coverage, worse at determinism seams and restraint consistency.
